The modular smart shelf is designed to detect and read RFID-tagged or labeled articles in real time using Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology. By integrating RFID functionality directly into the shelf structure, the system can identify items placed on or removed from the shelf without requiring manual scanning. This enables accurate inventory monitoring, improved product tracking, and enhanced interaction with retail or storage management systems.

The shelf includes a non-metallic, low-density core layer that forms the main structural body of the shelf. This core layer has opposed top and bottom faces, as well as an outer perimeter edge. The use of a non-metallic material helps reduce interference with radio frequency signals, allowing RFID signals to be transmitted and received more effectively through or around the shelf structure.

One or more antennae are disposed on the top face, the bottom face, or both faces of the core layer. These antennae are positioned to communicate with RFID tags or labels associated with articles placed on the shelf. To protect the antennae and provide a durable usable surface, a thermoplastic or resinous surface sheet is applied over the antennae. This covering may serve as a protective layer while also helping to maintain the shelf’s structural integrity and appearance.

In some configurations, the shelf may also include a molded frame secured around the outer perimeter edge of the core layer. The frame can provide additional mechanical strength, protect the edges of the shelf, and assist in mounting the shelf within a retail fixture, cabinet, or gondola system. The molded frame may also contribute to the overall finished appearance of the smart shelf module.

An RF transceiver is connected to the antennae to manage the transmission and reception of RFID signals. The transceiver communicates with RFID-tagged or labeled articles and may be linked to additional electronic components, including a front video display panel. The system may also connect with power and communication components located in a shelf gondola support base. Through these connections, the smart shelf can integrate RFID detection, product information display, power delivery, and data communication into a single modular shelf assembly.
outputs.L4:
A modular smart shelf is provided for use in retail, inventory, storage, and logistics environments where individual items are to be identified, monitored, and tracked in real time. The shelf is configured to detect and read items carrying radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags as the items are placed on, removed from, or moved across the shelf surface. By integrating RFID antenna structures directly into the shelf body, the system enables item-level visibility without requiring separate external reader fixtures or bulky add-on components.

The shelf may include a low-density, non-metallic core that provides structural support while allowing radio-frequency signals to propagate efficiently. Embedded within or positioned adjacent to this core are one or more RFID antennae arranged to create defined read zones across the shelf surface. The antennae may be configured to detect RFID-tagged merchandise located on the shelf and to communicate tag information to an associated RF transceiver. Because the core is non-metallic, it minimizes interference with RF fields and helps improve the reliability and accuracy of tag detection.

To protect the internal antenna structures and provide a durable product-support surface, the core and antennae may be covered by one or more thermoplastic, polymeric, or resinous surface sheets. These outer sheets may be selected for strength, wear resistance, ease of cleaning, and compatibility with retail shelving requirements. The resulting construction forms a thin, integrated shelf panel that can function both as a conventional load-bearing shelf and as an electronic sensing platform.

The smart shelf may further include an integrated frame or edge structure that supports the shelf panel and houses or routes electrical and communication components. The frame may include connectors for supplying power to the shelf, transmitting data, and linking multiple shelves together within a larger shelving bay or store-wide inventory system. In some embodiments, the connectors may allow the shelf to be installed, removed, or replaced in a modular manner, enabling rapid deployment and maintenance.

An RF transceiver may be incorporated into the shelf assembly or connected to the embedded antennae through the integrated wiring and connector system. The transceiver energizes RFID tags within the shelf’s read field and receives identifying information from the tags. The collected tag data may then be transmitted to a controller, point-of-sale system, inventory management platform, or cloud-based analytics system. This allows retailers or operators to monitor product availability, detect misplaced items, identify stock-outs, confirm planogram compliance, and obtain real-time inventory information.

The shelf may also include an optional display or indicator module. Such a display may present pricing, product information, stock status, shelf identification, promotional messaging, or diagnostic information relating to the RFID system. Visual indicators may also be used to assist store personnel in locating products, identifying items that require restocking, or confirming that the shelf is operating correctly.

In use, RFID-tagged items placed on the smart shelf are automatically detected by the embedded antennae. The shelf can continuously or periodically scan for tags and report changes in inventory status as they occur. When an item is removed, added, or relocated, the system can update the associated inventory records without requiring manual scanning. Multiple smart shelves may be connected together to form an intelligent shelving system capable of tracking items across an entire retail fixture, aisle, stockroom, or facility.

The modular construction of the shelf enables it to be incorporated into standard retail shelf systems while providing integrated power, communication, RFID reading, and optional display functionality. This design reduces installation complexity, protects the RFID components within the shelf structure, and provides a seamless smart-shelving solution for real-time item tracking and inventory management.
outputs.L5:
**Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)** is a technology that uses radio waves to identify, track, and manage objects, animals, or people. It works through a small electronic tag that contains stored information and a reader that sends and receives signals using a specific radio frequency.

An RFID system usually has two main parts: an RFID tag and an RFID reader. The tag is attached to an item and contains a microchip and antenna. When the tag enters the range of the reader, the reader sends out a radio signal. The tag responds by transmitting its identification data back to the reader. This process allows information to be collected quickly and without direct contact.

RFID is widely used in many industries. In retail, it helps track products, manage inventory, and reduce theft. In transportation, RFID cards are used for toll payments and public transit access. Hospitals use RFID to track medical equipment and patient records, while warehouses use it to improve logistics and supply chain efficiency.

One of the main advantages of Radio Frequency Identification is that it is faster and more convenient than traditional barcode scanning. RFID tags do not need to be seen directly by the reader, and multiple tags can be read at the same time. This makes the technology useful in situations where speed, accuracy, and automation are important.

Overall, RFID is an important modern identification technology. By combining radio signals, frequency-based communication, and digital identification, it helps businesses and organizations improve security, efficiency, and data management.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for a retail smart shelf using RFID antennas embedded in a non-metallic shelf structure, in the formal language of a patent specification.
counterfactuals.output:
## Title  
**Retail Smart Shelf Having RFID Antennas Embedded in a Non-Metallic Shelf Structure**

## Abstract  
A retail smart shelf is disclosed for identifying, locating, and monitoring merchandise disposed on a shelf surface. The shelf includes a non-metallic shelf body having one or more radio-frequency identification (RFID) antennas embedded within, laminated into, molded into, or otherwise integrated with the shelf structure. The non-metallic material permits transmission of radio-frequency energy while mechanically supporting retail products. The embedded antennas are coupled to an RFID reader, either directly or through a switching network or matching circuit, to interrogate RFID tags associated with items placed on the shelf. The shelf may include multiple antenna zones arranged along the length, width, or depth of the shelf to determine product presence, quantity, and approximate location. The construction protects the antennas from damage, reduces visual clutter, and enables inventory monitoring without requiring metallic brackets, exposed antenna panels, or externally mounted RFID hardware.

## Field of the Invention  
The present invention relates generally to retail inventory monitoring systems and, more particularly, to a smart shelf for retail environments incorporating radio-frequency identification antennas embedded in a non-metallic shelf structure.

## Background of the Invention  
Retailers frequently require accurate and timely information regarding the presence, quantity, and placement of products on store shelves. Conventional methods include manual counting, optical recognition, weight sensing, and RFID interrogation. Manual counting is labor-intensive and prone to delay. Optical systems can be affected by lighting, occlusion, packaging orientation, and customer interaction. Weight-based systems often require calibration for each product type and may be inaccurate where multiple products share a shelf.

RFID systems can identify individual tagged items without line-of-sight. However, conventional RFID shelf systems often require antennas to be mounted beneath, behind, or above a shelf. Such antennas may be visible, exposed to damage, difficult to retrofit, or impaired by metallic shelf components. In particular, metal shelf structures may detune antennas, shield RFID fields, or create unpredictable read zones. External antennas can also interfere with merchandising aesthetics and limit flexibility in product placement.

Accordingly, there is a need for a retail shelf construction that integrates RFID sensing capability into the shelf itself while maintaining a clean appearance, protecting antenna elements, and providing reliable RFID interrogation of items positioned on the shelf.

## Summary of the Invention  
In one embodiment, a retail smart shelf includes a shelf body formed at least in part from a non-metallic material, such as plastic, composite, fiberglass, wood-based material, resin, glass-reinforced polymer, ceramic-filled polymer, or other dielectric material. One or more RFID antennas are embedded within the shelf body and are positioned to radiate through an upper support surface of the shelf toward RFID-tagged products resting on the shelf.

In another embodiment, the shelf body includes a top layer, a bottom layer, and an intermediate core layer. One or more antenna elements are disposed between the layers and are encapsulated by the shelf material. The antenna elements may be formed as conductive traces, wires, foils, printed conductive ink, etched conductive films, flexible printed circuits, or molded conductors.

In a further embodiment, the shelf includes a plurality of embedded RFID antennas defining respective read zones. The read zones may correspond to shelf positions, product lanes, planogram locations, or depth regions extending from a front edge toward a rear edge of the shelf. An RFID reader may selectively energize the antennas through a multiplexer to obtain item identity and location information.

In another embodiment, the smart shelf includes antenna tuning components, impedance matching elements, shielding or field-shaping structures, cable routing channels, connectors, and an integrated controller. The smart shelf may communicate inventory data to a point-of-sale system, store server, planogram management system, or cloud-based inventory platform.

The invention thus provides an unobtrusive and durable RFID-enabled shelf structure suitable for retail inventory monitoring, shelf replenishment detection, misplaced item detection, theft deterrence, product localization, and customer interaction analytics.

## Brief Description of the Drawings  
The accompanying drawings, if provided, illustrate exemplary embodiments of the invention and are not intended to limit the scope of the disclosure.

**FIG. 1** is a perspective view of a retail smart shelf having RFID antennas embedded in a non-metallic shelf body.  

**FIG. 2** is an exploded cross-sectional view of a laminated shelf structure including embedded antenna elements.  

**FIG. 3** is a top plan view showing a plurality of antenna zones disposed along the length and depth of the shelf.  

**FIG. 4** is a schematic diagram of an RFID reader coupled to embedded antennas through a switching network.  

**FIG. 5** is a cross-sectional view of an embodiment including a recessed cable channel and connector at a rear portion of the shelf.

## Detailed Description of Exemplary Embodiments  
Referring generally to the embodiments described herein, a smart shelf is provided for use in a retail environment, such as a grocery store, pharmacy, apparel store, electronics store, warehouse club, convenience store, or stockroom. The smart shelf is configured to support merchandise and to interrogate RFID tags affixed to, incorporated in, or otherwise associated with the merchandise.

The smart shelf includes a shelf body having an upper surface configured to support retail products, a lower surface, a front edge, a rear edge, and opposing side edges. The shelf body is formed at least partially from a non-metallic material. As used herein, “non-metallic” refers to a material that is substantially non-conductive at RFID operating frequencies and that does not substantially shield or detune an RFID antenna embedded therein. Suitable materials include, without limitation, polymeric materials, thermoplastics, thermoset resins, fiber-reinforced plastics, wood, engineered wood, laminated composites, glass, ceramics, and combinations thereof.

At least one RFID antenna is embedded within the shelf body. The antenna may be fully encapsulated within the non-metallic material or may be disposed in an internal recess, channel, cavity, or laminated interface of the shelf body. By embedding the antenna within the shelf structure, the antenna is protected from abrasion, impact, cleaning fluids, tampering, and incidental contact with merchandise or customers.

The RFID antenna may be configured for operation in any suitable RFID frequency band, including low frequency (LF), high frequency (HF), near-field UHF, or far-field UHF. In a preferred retail embodiment, the antenna is configured for UHF RFID operation, for example in the range of approximately 860 MHz to 960 MHz, although other frequencies may be used depending on regulatory region and application.

The antenna may comprise a dipole, patch antenna, slot antenna, loop antenna, meandered trace, near-field coupler, microstrip element, leaky wave structure, distributed antenna, or other radiating or coupling structure. In some embodiments, the antenna is formed on a flexible printed circuit substrate and laminated between layers of the shelf body. In other embodiments, the antenna is printed directly on a shelf layer using conductive ink and subsequently overmolded or covered by a protective dielectric layer.

In one embodiment, the shelf body comprises a laminated structure including an upper dielectric panel, a lower dielectric panel, and an intermediate layer containing the antenna. The antenna may be bonded to one of the panels prior to lamination. Adhesive layers may be selected to have dielectric properties compatible with antenna operation. The thickness of the upper dielectric panel may be selected to provide mechanical durability while permitting efficient coupling between the antenna and RFID tags located on products positioned above the shelf.

In another embodiment, the shelf body is molded around one or more antenna inserts. For example, a conductive antenna pattern may be carried on a flexible substrate and placed in a mold before injection molding, compression molding, or resin casting the non-metallic shelf body. The resulting structure integrates the antenna into the shelf without exposed fasteners or externally visible antenna hardware.

A plurality of antennas may be embedded within the shelf body. The antennas may be arranged in a linear array along the shelf length, in a two-dimensional array across the shelf surface, or in lanes extending from the front edge to the rear edge of the shelf. Each antenna may define a corresponding interrogation zone. By selectively energizing individual antennas and analyzing tag responses, the system may determine whether an RFID-tagged item is located in a particular zone. The zones may correspond to expected product positions defined by a retail planogram.

The embedded antennas may be coupled to an RFID reader through coaxial cables, balanced transmission lines, microstrip lines, stripline conductors, or other suitable conductive paths. Such conductive paths may also be embedded in the shelf body or routed through internal channels. A connector may be positioned at the rear edge or underside of the shelf to permit connection to an RFID reader, shelf controller, power supply, or network interface.

In certain embodiments, the shelf includes an antenna switching network. The switching network may be disposed within the shelf, on the underside of the shelf, at a rear rail, or in a separate electronics module. The switching network selectively connects one or more embedded antennas to an RFID reader. The switching network may include RF switches, multiplexers, relays, impedance matching networks, filters, couplers, or tuning elements. The RFID reader may sequentially energize antennas to scan multiple shelf zones using a single reader port.

The smart shelf may further include a controller configured to operate the RFID reader, process tag-read data, and transmit inventory information to a retail information system. The controller may determine item presence, item count, dwell time, removal events, restocking events, misplaced product events, and out-of-stock conditions. The controller may compare detected tag identities and locations with stored planogram data to determine whether products are located in expected positions.

In some embodiments, the shelf includes field-shaping features. For example, non-metallic dielectric structures may be positioned above or around the antenna to direct RFID energy toward the support surface. In embodiments where metal support brackets or store gondola structures are present, the shelf may include spacing members, dielectric standoffs, localized ground structures, absorptive materials, or tuned reflectors arranged to reduce undesirable coupling to nearby metal. Any conductive structures used for field shaping may be positioned so as not to negate the advantage of the non-metallic shelf body and may be electrically isolated from the embedded antenna as required.

The shelf may include a front label rail, product divider attachment features, lighting, electronic shelf labels, or customer-facing displays. The embedded RFID antennas may be positioned to avoid interference with such components. In certain embodiments, the front portion of the shelf includes a first antenna zone configured to detect product removal from the front of the shelf, while a rear portion includes another antenna zone configured to determine remaining stock depth.

The system may operate according to a periodic scanning mode, an event-triggered mode, or a continuous monitoring mode. In periodic scanning, the RFID reader interrogates the embedded antennas at selected intervals. In event-triggered operation, scanning may be initiated by a motion sensor, door opening sensor, weight sensor, optical sensor, point-of-sale event, or inventory management command. In continuous monitoring, the system repeatedly scans the shelf to detect item movement in near real time.

The non-metallic shelf body may be dimensioned to replace conventional retail shelving and may be compatible with standard gondola uprights, brackets, or shelf supports. The shelf may include reinforced non-metallic ribs, internal honeycomb structures, composite beams, or edge stiffeners to provide load-bearing capacity. In embodiments where reinforcement is required, reinforcement materials may be selected or positioned to reduce interference with RFID operation.

The embedded configuration offers several advantages. The antennas are concealed and protected, improving durability and appearance. The non-metallic shelf body reduces RF shielding and detuning relative to metal shelves. Multiple antenna zones can be incorporated without external antenna panels. The shelf can be manufactured as a modular component and connected to existing RFID readers or store networks. The system enables more accurate inventory visibility at the shelf level and may support automated replenishment and planogram compliance.

Although specific embodiments have been described, the invention is not limited to the particular configurations disclosed. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features of another embodiment. The number, shape, frequency, orientation, and placement of antennas may be varied according to shelf size, product type, tag orientation, desired read range, and regulatory requirements. The scope of the invention is intended to encompass all modifications and equivalents consistent with the disclosure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise technical summary of a modular shelf capable of reading RFID-tagged products placed on or near it, mentioning construction materials, antenna integration, electronics, and power/communications connections.
counterfactuals.output:
A modular RFID-enabled shelf is constructed as a rigid panel or tray using materials such as plastic, wood, composite laminate, glass, or metal with appropriate RF isolation layers. One or more RFID antennas are embedded, bonded, printed, or mounted within the shelf surface, underside, rear edge, or side rails to create a read zone covering products placed on or near the shelf.

The shelf includes integrated electronics such as an RFID reader or reader interface, antenna matching/tuning circuitry, multiplexers for multiple antennas, shielding or ferrite layers to control field direction, and optional sensors or indicators. The antenna layout may be optimized to detect item-level RFID tags while limiting reads from adjacent shelves or nearby areas.

Power and data are supplied through modular connectors, edge contacts, cable harnesses, or a backplane integrated into the shelving structure. Communications may use Ethernet, USB, RS-485, CAN, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or similar interfaces to report tag reads to a local controller or inventory management system. Multiple shelves can be daisy-chained or independently addressed to support scalable inventory tracking in retail, warehouse, laboratory, or smart-cabinet applications.

counterfactuals.prompt: In one paragraph, explain the design of an RFID-enabled modular shelf for a store gondola, including antennae on the shelf faces, an RF transceiver in the rear frame, and connectors for power, communications, and a display panel.
counterfactuals.output: An RFID-enabled modular shelf for a store gondola can be designed as a self-contained shelving module that both supports merchandise and identifies tagged items placed on it. RFID antennae are integrated along the front or face portions of the shelf, positioned to read tags on products across the shelf surface while minimizing interference with adjacent shelves. These antennae are wired back through the shelf structure to an RF transceiver housed in the rear frame of the module, where the transceiver energizes the antennae, receives RFID tag responses, and processes or forwards item-detection data. The rear frame also includes standardized connectors that allow the shelf to be quickly installed, removed, or daisy-chained with other shelves, providing power, data communications to a store network or controller, and an interface for a display panel such as an electronic shelf label or promotional screen mounted at the front of the shelf. This modular arrangement enables inventory monitoring, planogram compliance, and customer-facing digital information while keeping the electronics protected and installation simple.
